summary: Patrick Debois introduces the thesis that context is the new code, drawing a parallel to his 2009 DevOps movement. As AI coding agents proliferate, the prompts, rules, and memory driving them require engineering rigor. He proposes the Context Development Lifecycle as an infinity loop: Generate, Evaluate, Distribute, and Observe. Under Generate, he covers prompting, reusable prompts via agent.md standardization, pulling library documentation to prevent hallucination, MCP integrations, and spec-driven development. Under Evaluate, he draws parallels to code testing levels: linting for format, Grammarly-style comprehension checks, LLM-as-judge for convention adherence, unit-test-like suites, end-to-end sandboxed tests, per-commit impact measurement, and automated context optimization. He warns evals are non-deterministic, recommending multiple runs and error budgets. Under Distribute, he moves beyond checking context into version control to packaging context like libraries, with registries and marketplaces such as the Tessl registry. He notes 99.9% of published skills are low quality but useful for learning. Context packages face dependency hell, versioning, and security concerns including SBOM-style provenance, Snyk-style context scanning, and awareness of who built a skill and with what model. Under Observe, he describes using agent logs to detect missing context across teams, treating incomplete PR feedback as context feedback, and instrumenting production code to trace failures back to context gaps. He introduces context filters as a web-application-firewall-like layer against prompt injection, since sandboxes cannot block auto-loaded agent.md files. He describes two improvement loops: an individual authoring loop and an organizational loop where teams share and maintain context like libraries. The context flywheel emerges when better context produces better agent output, yielding better observations that improve context again. He frames LLMs as engines and context as fuel—the part practitioners can optimize. In Q&A, he acknowledges that investing rigorously in context means significant time building the right evals, and notes consistency across parallel agent runs as a potential eval technique.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Context is becoming as important as code and needs its own engineering discipline, paralleling how DevOps formalized ops practices.
The Context Development Lifecycle consists of four phases in an infinity loop: Generate, Evaluate, Distribute, and Observe.
Reusable prompts, library docs, MCP integrations, and spec-driven development are key context generation strategies.
Context testing parallels code testing: linting, LLM-as-judge, unit-test-like suites, and sandboxed end-to-end tests, with error budgets for non-determinism.
Context distribution evolves from version control to packaged libraries, registries, dependency management, and security scanning with AI SBOM provenance.
Agent logs, PR feedback, and production instrumentation serve as observation channels to detect missing or broken context.
Context filters act like a web application firewall against prompt injection, since sandboxes cannot block auto-loaded context files.
Two improvement loops exist: individual context authoring and organizational sharing, forming a context flywheel across teams.
LLMs are engines and context is fuel—practitioners cannot change the LLM but can optimize context in an engineered way.
Investing rigorously in context means significant time building the right evals, which itself becomes a process to engineer.

sections.title: Introduction and audience poll
sections.summary: Debois opens the architect track and polls the audience on AI coding agent usage, noting that very few people have not used them.

sections.title: Why context is the new code
sections.summary: Debois explains he now barely touches code, instead directing AI agents through context. He describes converting large code helpers into reusable skills that handle onboarding workflows. He draws a parallel to DevOps in 2009, proposing context needs the same formal treatment.

sections.title: Introducing the Context Development Lifecycle
sections.summary: Debois introduces the Context Development Lifecycle as an infinity loop: Generate, Evaluate, Distribute, and Observe, with adapt and regenerate closing the loop, mirroring the DevOps infinity loop.

sections.title: Generate: Creating context for agents
sections.summary: Covers human prompting, reusable prompts via agent.md standardization (noting Claude still uses Claude.md), pulling library documentation to prevent hallucination, using MCP to pull context from GitLab, GitHub, and Slack, and spec-driven development where agents break specifications into step-by-step plans.

sections.title: Evaluate: Testing your context
sections.summary: Draws parallels to code testing levels: linting for context format validation, Grammarly-style comprehension checks, LLM-as-judge for convention adherence (demonstrated with /awesome prefix), unit-test-like suites, end-to-end tests via sandboxed agent execution with tools, per-commit context impact testing, automated context optimization using LLM feedback, and error budgets for non-determinism.

sections.title: Distribute: Sharing and packaging context
sections.summary: Begins with checking context into version control for zero-friction sharing, then extends to packaging context like libraries with registries and marketplaces. Notes 99.9% of registry skills are low quality but useful for learning. Addresses dependency hell when combining context packages, versioning, security scanning (Snyk-style), and AI SBOM provenance capturing who built a skill and with what model.

sections.title: Observe: Monitoring and feedback loops
sections.summary: Covers using agent logs to detect missing context across teams, treating incomplete PR feedback as context feedback, instrumenting production code to trace failures back to context gaps and generate test cases, sandboxing agents for security testing, and introducing context filters as a web-application-firewall-like layer against prompt injection since sandboxes cannot block auto-loaded agent.md files. References harness engineering observability.

sections.title: Conclusion and the context flywheel
sections.summary: Describes two improvement loops: individual context authoring and organizational sharing across teams, forming a context flywheel. Frames LLMs as engines and context as fuel—the part practitioners can optimize. Promotes Tessl and AI DevCon conference.

sections.title: Q&A session
sections.summary: Audience question about exotic context forms and using consistency across parallel agent runs as an eval technique. Debois acknowledges the approach and emphasizes that rigorous context engineering means significant time invested in building the right evals, which advanced practitioners treat as their own process.
